content:
Even though Apple has tried to keep Jony Ive at arm's length in its lawsuit against OpenAI, the company may not be able to stop its former design chief from getting pulled into the dispute. Here's why.

OpenAI has a chance to make Apple very uncomfortable

In its lawsuit accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets, Apple has conspicuously avoided mentioning Jony Ive. Ive's company, io Products, partnered with OpenAI on the hardware Apple alleges is at the centre of the case.

Apple has accused "OpenAI and its co-conspirators of engaging in organised misconduct at an institutional level," a description that includes io, but Apple refers to it only as "a business co-founded by Mr Tang and other former Apple executives." Beyond that, the complaint does not name Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executive — except Tang Tan and Chang Liu, who are directly accused of wrongdoing.

While it's too early to say whether Ive will be called to testify, it is certainly a possibility, especially if OpenAI decides to use him to embarrass or discomfort Apple.

That would put Apple in an unusually delicate position. Since leaving the company in 2019, Ive has been publicly respectful toward Apple, and his appearances and visits have typically been carefully staged.

Those have included joint appearances with Laurene Powell Jobs and ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive contributed a personal letter to the archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" series, reflecting on his time working with Steve Jobs.

Apple, for its part, has also responded in kind, deliberately reassessing several controversial decisions tied to the final years of Ive's tenure, including the MacBook's butterfly keyboard. The attempt to keep some distance from him in the lawsuit is consistent with that approach.

But Apple won't fully control who gets pulled in once the case moves into discovery. Given Ive's role in founding io Products and overseeing the hardware project at issue, OpenAI could argue that he has relevant knowledge about how the product was developed, what information the team relied on, and whether Apple's trade secrets played a part.

Apple could then face the awkward prospect of cross-examining Ive in court, challenging his account, or trying to undermine the credibility of the executive who shaped many of Apple's most iconic products.

It wouldn't be the first time Ive has testified in litigation involving Apple. Back in 2012, his deposition was taken in an Apple patent case, where he answered questions about the company's design process and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

However, taking the stand on the opposing side could strain the carefully maintained relationship he has kept with Apple, and it could also create friction with OpenAI if Ive feels the company has unnecessarily dragged him into the dispute to pressure his former employer.

Do you think Jony Ive will get pulled into this lawsuit? Let us know in the comments.
